feedback: D1 is a solid but incomplete catalogue. You nailed F1 SQL injection with the concatenated query at lines 64-67 and the 02:15:31 admin' OR '1'='1 to 302 capture, plus clean writeups of XXE (04-import-xxe.xml file:///etc/passwd), stored XSS (02:18:47 cookie beacon to 185.220.101.9:8443), path traversal (02:24:02 root:x:0:0:), and the no-expiry token. Where you lost points: alg:none is tagged CWE-34 when it should be CWE-347, and you only mention unsalted MD5 (CWE-916) and the hardcoded secret sankofa-legacy-admin-2019 (CWE-798) in passing prose rather than cataloguing them as their own findings, and you never found the open redirect ?next= (02:21:13, CWE-601) or the cookie missing Secure/SameSite (CWE-614). That is six of ten, so D1 cannot reach the high band. The decoy is the weakest part: the safe construct in this pack is the HS256 verify branch using hash_equals(), which is constant-time and therefore sound, or the b64url encoding helpers. You instead picked the username-reflection error message and your verdict (not exploitable because it confirms which usernames exist) confuses username enumeration with XSS and does not prove anything safe at the mechanism level, so that row earns almost nothing. Good news is you did not fall into the trap of labelling alg:none the decoy, which would have been wrong, so no penalty there. D2 is your strongest deliverable. The chain is in order with verbatim PoC at each hop (the SQLi body, the XSS fetch payload, the full XXE XML, the path-traversal request) and most hops reconcile to a real capture line. Two issues hold it back: your F1 CVSS vector is AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H scoring 9.8, but the auth bypass does not affect availability, so it should be A:N giving roughly 9.1, and several vectors arrive as a bare score with the per-metric justification thin. Your impact section is reasonable: 312 customers, the 20-row sample at 4,040,232 naira extrapolated to about 63M, tied to the BoltCash launch in six weeks, with your averaging assumption stated, which is exactly the reward-your-assumptions behaviour we want. D3 reads cleanly and the threat model is good, including the sharp observation that the shared /api/v1/internal service honours the same compromised token. But the exec summary calls the panel a Django app when the source is PHP, the findings section repeats only name and class without re-tying each to its evidence line, and your earliest-break reasoning is muddled (the earliest break is the SQLi at 02:15:31, not F2/F3). Credit where due: your remediation table is genuinely ordered with an effort column and you rank the 9.8 SQLi third behind faster JWT and XXE fixes, which is effort-to-risk thinking rather than blind CVSS ordering, so that row scores well. Your two detection stopgaps name a field (login POST body OR keyword, alg:none prefix) but give qualitative false-positive rates (Low, None) rather than an estimated rate, which costs a little. D4 is strong and in your own voice, answering all four prompts, citing ISC2 Canon I and Canon III by number in a load-bearing way, and anchoring to your own /legacy-admin quarantine recommendation. The gap is that you reference NDPA 2023 and the 72-hour duty but never name the section: that 72-hour notify-NDPC duty is section 40, and notifying the 312 affected data subjects on high risk is section 41, and naming those sections is what the rubric rewards. I looked for a way to push this into the 70s and the evidence did not support it, because four of the ten findings are absent and the decoy is misidentified. The single most important fix: catalogue all ten findings as discrete entries with the correct CWE (MD5 916, hardcoded secret 798, open redirect 601, cookie 614) and correctly disprove the hash_equals branch as the safe decoy at the mechanism level.
